chapter_theme: Under the heading அவையறிதல், nine verses on knowing the assembly: the skilled speaker reads his hearers' desire, does not answer back or speak out of turn, and wastes no counsel on fools, while the unlearned and shameless who push into the company of the wise talk emptily, mock the restraint of the learned, and are silent among the good but boastful among the mean.

17.reading: The skilled speak only after seeking out their hearers and learning what they want in the matter to be spoken, as bees go where their desire leads, for no one carries into an assembly the things that will lose there.
17.nuance: The verse makes the hearers' desire (வேட்கை), not the truth of the matter, the speaker's first measure; the bee image in line 3 repeats வேட்கை so that the speaker's skill is to follow desire as the bee follows scent. The address to a woman (வாட்கண்ணாய்!) is a frame.

pazhamozhi.literal: people do not enter an assembly carrying things that will be defeated

story.act: no story; the proverb states what anyone entering a contest of an assembly avoids

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speech that does not meet the hearers' desire is a losing case brought into the assembly

18.reading: When one person has spoken his piece, it is not fitting to take it up and answer back so that the two become opponents, for, lord of the great-hilled land, it goes ill even a little when two dogs play together.
18.nuance: The proverb's point is that dogs' play turns into a fight; a counter-reply in assembly is play of the same kind. Lines 1-2 are compressed and could also be read as forbidding a second man to join in answering one speaker; the reading takes இருவரா as the exchange becoming a two-sided quarrel.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is unpleasant when two dogs play together

story.act: no story; two dogs at play, which soon fall to snarling

pazhamozhi.applied_to: answering back a speaker in assembly turns discussion into a quarrel

19.reading: In an exchange two men have closely begun, if the one whose turn is to speak afterwards pushes forward and speaks first, his is the talk of one who does not know speech, like wrapping the nose of a man whose knee is torn.
19.nuance: The proverb mocks a remedy put on the wrong place: speaking out of turn answers what has not yet been raised and misses the wound. பின்னை உரைக்கப் படற்பாலான் may instead mean the one who is to be addressed later; on either reading the fault is pre-empting the order of the exchange.

pazhamozhi.literal: bandaging the nose of a man whose knee is torn

story.act: no story; a misplaced dressing for an injury elsewhere

pazhamozhi.applied_to: speaking before one's turn in a dispute misses the point at issue

20.reading: Those who, having neither learnt nor listened, bandy words in the midst of an assembly of the learned are themselves to be feared, lord of the hills where bright cascades leap, for even the gods have no power against those who have lost all decency.
20.nuance: The fear runs the unexpected way: not the unlearned fearing the learned, but the learned well advised to fear the unlearned talker, because shamelessness (பரிசழிந்தார்) cannot be answered by argument. The verse joins the two routes of 11, study and listening, as what these talkers lack.

pazhamozhi.literal: even the gods are powerless against those who have lost their decency

story.act: no story; the proverb sets the shameless beyond even divine power

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the learned cannot prevail over shameless unlearned talkers and should avoid them

21.reading: Those who, not knowing how to enter, have entered among men of broad understanding and then out of contentiousness utter empty, mean words are doing just what the saying of the bards' quarter and its talk of teeth describes.
21.nuance: The proverb's sense is not clear from the words: பாண்சேரி பற்கிளக்குமாறு is 'the way the bards' quarter tells of teeth', perhaps boasting of what the poor have chewed, or teeth to be lost in a quarrel; the reading leaves it open. The verse's own counsel, that entering without knowing how leads to vain contention, is clear.

pazhamozhi.literal: the way the bards' quarter speaks of teeth

story.act: an allusion to a saying about the bards' street and teeth whose point the verse does not spell out

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the empty contentious talk of one who has pushed in among the wise

22.reading: For those who know neither honour nor shame, their minds confused, to enter among men who know wisdom, sit there and speak questioning that wisdom is laughable, like the venture of one who goes in to see an elephant's tusk.
22.nuance: The verse puts the fault in character before learning: it is the lack of மானம் and நாண் that lets the man sit among the wise and question them. The proverb may hold a pun, since நகை is both laughter and teeth: one who would see an elephant's tusk must get close to a dangerous thing, and the attempt is absurd.

pazhamozhi.literal: laughable is the going-in of one who wants to see an elephant's tusk

story.act: no story; a man pushing close to an elephant to inspect its tusk

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the shameless man who questions the wise makes himself ridiculous

23.reading: Those who live chattering in bad assemblies, when they enter a good assembly and speak scorning the knowledge of men whose learning has passed all measure and keeps their tongues in check, are like a man eager to eat weevil-eaten pepper.
23.nuance: The learned are silent because of their learning (நாவடங்கக் கல்வி அளவிறந்து மிக்கார்), and the chatterer reads that silence as emptiness and mocks it. The proverb (மிளகுளு, worm-eaten pepper) seems to mean relishing what has no savour left, but its point is not certain.

pazhamozhi.literal: the eagerness of one who eats worm-eaten pepper

story.act: no story; a man relishing spoiled pepper

pazhamozhi.applied_to: the chatterer's mockery of the restrained learned is a taste for what is worthless

24.reading: To roll up one's tongue on seeing a good assembly and then praise oneself in a mean assembly that does not understand the good is the way of a man who, afraid of the fierce flank of his enemies, strings his bow inside his house and shoots at the pot in the middle of it.
24.nuance: The verse pairs two faults as one: silence from fear before the good and self-praise before the mean are the same cowardice, brave only where nothing answers back. The proverb's bow drawn at home against a household pot is the clearest image in the chapter.

pazhamozhi.literal: stringing a bow inside the house and shooting at the pot in its middle

story.act: a man who fears to face the enemy's fierce side shows his archery at home on a pot

pazhamozhi.applied_to: silent among the good and boastful among the mean is cowardice that performs where it is safe

25.reading: To speak sound counsel to someone in a crowded assembly of thoroughly dull men who, untroubled, do not grasp the good, is like sifting flour in the sea.
25.nuance: நடலை இலராகி (being without trouble or pretence) and உடலா ஒருவற்கு (to one who does not dispute, or does not agree) are both doubtful; the reading takes the first as the fools' complacency and the second as the hearer counselled. The proverb's loss is total: the flour is not spoiled but simply gone.

pazhamozhi.literal: like sifting flour in the sea

story.act: no story; flour strained into the sea is lost

pazhamozhi.applied_to: counsel spoken among dull men is wholly lost

links.note: Kural 711 bids the speaker know the assembly and examine the matter before speaking; Pazhamozhi 17 names what is to be known, the hearers' desire about the matter, and calls speech that misses it a losing case.
links.teaches: Read together, knowing the assembly turns out to mean reading its appetite: the Kural asks for discernment, and Pazhamozhi says that discernment is of desire, so a true speech the hearers do not want is already lost.
links.list_adds: its bee image and proverb make the hearers' want the measure and recast unsuited speech as a defeat carried into the contest.

links.note: Kural 715 praises the restraint of not speaking first among elders; Pazhamozhi 19 applies the same rule of order to a dispute two have begun, where the later speaker pushes ahead of his turn.
links.teaches: The pair shows the Kural's rule of precedence is also a rule of relevance: speaking out of turn is not only immodest but misses the point at issue, as the bandage misses the torn knee.
links.list_adds: the proverb gives a reason the couplet lacks: speech before its turn lands on the wrong place.

links.note: Kural 729 holds the learned who fear an assembly of the good lower than the unlearned; Pazhamozhi 20 advises the learned to fear the unlearned who bandy words among them.
links.teaches: The Kural's demand for fearlessness in assembly has an exception: before the good, fear is a failing, but before the shameless unlearned, against whom even gods are powerless, wariness is wisdom.
links.list_adds: it names the one opponent in an assembly a learned man should fear, and its proverb grounds that fear in shamelessness rather than skill.

links.note: Naladiyar 314's fool, with one overheard sutra, walks unabashed (நாணாது) into the gathering of the good and shows his petty understanding; Pazhamozhi 22's man, knowing neither honour nor shame, sits among the wise and questions them.
links.teaches: Both trace the intrusion to a lack of shame rather than of learning alone, and Pazhamozhi adds that the shameless man need not even recite: questioning the wise is enough to make him laughable.
links.list_adds: it pairs மானம் with நாண் as what is missing and turns the exposure into ridicule through its proverb.

links.note: Naladiyar 255 praises the worthy who will not speak their learning even when asked, knowing it would not be taken in; Pazhamozhi 23 shows the chatterer scorning those whose learning keeps their tongues in check.
links.teaches: The pair exposes the cost of the worthy's silence that the Naladiyar praises: the low read restraint as emptiness and mock it, so the learned man's silence protects his learning but not his standing.
links.list_adds: it sets the restrained learned and the chattering intruder in one scene, so the silence the quatrain commends is seen from the scoffer's side.

links.note: Kural 719 tells the able speaker not to speak in a mean assembly even by slip; Pazhamozhi 24 condemns the man who does the reverse, silent before the good and boastful before the mean.
links.teaches: The pair fixes both halves of the rule: the Kural forbids good speech wasted on the mean, Pazhamozhi shows the inverted vice, where the mean assembly gets self-praise and the good assembly gets nothing.
links.list_adds: it joins silence among the good and self-praise among the mean as one fault and gives it a single image of cowardice.

links.note: Kural 727 likens the learning of one who fears the assembly to a bright sword in a பேடி's hand amid enemies; Pazhamozhi 24 likens the same fear to a man who strings his bow at home and shoots a pot.
links.teaches: The two martial images complete each other: the Kural shows the weapon useless in the field, Pazhamozhi shows it used where no enemy is, so fear of the assembly is both impotence before the learned and bravado before the mean.
links.list_adds: it adds the self-praise in a mean assembly to the fear the couplet names, so the coward's display is seen alongside his failure.

links.note: Kural 720 likens holding forth before those not of one's group to nectar spilled in a dirty yard; Pazhamozhi 25 likens counsel spoken among dull men to sifting flour in the sea.
links.teaches: The two waste images differ in what is lost: the Kural's nectar is fouled where it falls, Pazhamozhi's flour simply vanishes, and Pazhamozhi names the hearers as fools rather than outsiders, so the loss comes from incapacity, not from difference of group.
links.list_adds: it narrows the couplet's 'those not of one's group' to the dull and complacent and makes the counsel itself (உறுதி), not display, what is lost.

links.note: Innaa Narpathu 10 counts, as its first painful thing, reciting a song where none grasp its meaning as painful; Pazhamozhi 25 says counsel spoken among dull men is lost like flour sifted in the sea.
links.teaches: The counted work names the speaker's pain and the proverb names the speech's loss, so together they show that speaking to those who cannot take it in hurts the speaker and achieves nothing for the hearer.

links.note: Verse 18 forbids answering back so that an exchange becomes a two-sided quarrel; verse 19 forbids pushing ahead of one's turn in an exchange two have begun.
links.teaches: Read in sequence the two verses give a small order of debate in assembly: do not turn a speech into a contest by retort, and do not break into a contest out of turn.

source_issues: 21 line 4: the proverb opens with a quotation mark ('பாண்சேரி) that is never closed.
21 line 4: பாண்சேரி பற்கிளக்கு மாறு is obscure, and the proverb's sense is unclear from the text.
23 line 4: மிளகுளு வுண்பான் (worm-eaten pepper) is obscure, and the proverb's point is uncertain.
25 lines 1-3: நடலை இலராகி and உடலா ஒருவற்கு are of doubtful sense.
